title: Aesthetics PPL + Arms: Periodized
subtitle: 12 weeks, 7 sessions per week, RIR ramping inside three volume blocks
summary: The maximum-effort split: Legs, Push, Pull, Legs, Push, Pull and an Arms day. Volume steps up every 4 weeks (10, then 12, then 15 working sets) while effort ramps from 3-4 RIR down to 0 RIR inside each block.
progressionNotes: Progressive overload inside the given rep range. About 2.5 lbs per week on the compound movements. For isolation work, set a rep goal you must hit at a given weight (for example 8, 10, 12, then 15 reps) before you increase it.

guide.heading: How the 12 weeks are built
body: Weeks 1-4 use 10 working sets, weeks 5-8 use 12, and weeks 9-12 use 15. Inside each 4-week block your effort ramps up: Week 1 at 3-4 RIR, Week 2 at 2 RIR, Week 3 at 1 RIR, Week 4 at 0 RIR, then the next block starts back at 3-4 RIR.
Progressive overload at the given RIR each week. If you are a beginner you can ignore the RIR ramp and just train hard within the rep range.

guide.heading: Your split calendar
body: The full split runs on a 10-day cycle: Legs, Push, Pull, Rest, Legs, Push, Pull, Rest, Arms, Rest. That is 7 training sessions per program week: Legs (quad dominant), Push (chest dominant), Pull (width dominant), Legs (hams and glutes dominant), Push (shoulder dominant), Pull (thickness dominant) and Arms.
If you struggle with consistency, start with Legs, Push and Pull spread across the week (for example Monday, Wednesday and Friday, with Arms on Sunday) and work your way up.
If you want it as a weekly split, run Legs, Push, Pull, Legs, Push, Pull. This is very intense, so think about lowering the working sets for each muscle group.
The app assigns sessions to your training days in order, so the week counter follows sessions rather than the calendar.
Reach each weekly working set goal across the week. For example, with a goal of 15 sets for chest, do 10 on the first push day and 5 on the second.

guide.heading: Which program suits you
body: If you want the maximum gains and are willing to put the effort in, choose this PPL Arms split.

Periodized or linear? If you are a beginner (under 1-2 years of lifting) and not interested in the science, go for the Linear version. If you are interested in exercise science, go for the Periodized version. They have no additional benefits over each other; some people just like the look of the periodized split more.

guide.heading: Advanced: progression for the main lifts
body: For the main compound lifts you can also add a set each week inside the block, at a fixed percentage of your 1RM.
10 working sets, at 80% 1RM (weeks 1-4): Incline bench 3x8, 4x8, 5x8, 5x8. Rows 3x8, 4x8, 5x8, 5x8. Squat 3x6, 4x6, 5x6, 5x6. RDL 3x6, 4x6, 5x6, 5x6. Overhead press (optional) 3x8, 4x8, 5x10, 5x8.

12 working sets, at 75% 1RM (weeks 5-8): Incline bench 3x10, 4x10, 5x10, 5x10. Rows 3x10, 4x10, 5x10, 5x10. Squat 3x8, 4x8, 5x8, 5x8. RDL 3x8, 4x8, 5x8, 5x8. Overhead press (optional) 3x10, 4x10, 5x10, 5x10.

15 working sets, at 70% 1RM (weeks 9-12): Incline bench 3x12, 4x12, 5x12, 5x12. Rows 3x12, 4x12, 5x12, 5x12. Squat 3x10, 4x10, 5x10, 5x10. RDL 3x10, 4x10, 5x10, 5x10. Overhead press (optional) 3x12, 4x12, 5x12, 5x12.
Note that the sets on the sessions below already meet the weekly working set goal; if you use this progression, adjust the other exercises so the weekly total still matches the goal.

guide.heading: HIT block (not for beginners)
body: The HIT block is a desensitizing period after the volume progression built up through the split. Its working sets should be half of your MAV (the working sets in week 5), and it is a great way to stimulate your muscles in a different manner.
Take all sets to absolute failure. To choose the correct weight for the few sets you have, do 3 warm-up sets. Rest-pause and partials are better than assisted reps, so use them on all exercises.

guide.heading: Small tweak for shrugs
body: Instead of doing shrugs, do Kelso shrugs after a rowing movement, preferably a seated machine row, and replace the shrug working sets with Kelso shrugs.

guide.heading: How hard to train
body: General principle: more sets means do not train to failure (2-3 reps in reserve). Fewer sets means train to failure, or 1 rep in reserve.
Always try to progressively overload within the given rep range. A general guideline is 2.5 lbs per week, better applied to the compound movements.

An easy, simple way to progressively overload is to set a rep goal you must hit at a given weight before you increase it. For example, if you currently fail at 8 reps with a 50 lb barbell curl, next week aim for 10, then 12, then 15. When you hit 15, you can increase the weight. For isolation exercises that do not follow the progression scheme, I recommend this approach; the rep goal I recommend is 12-15.

guide.heading: Adjusting your volume
body: As you gain experience, auto-adjust your working sets, for example 10, then 12, then 15 instead of 8, 10, 12.

Decrease sets if you are getting weaker in every movement for a muscle. Increase sets if you have plateaued: after several weeks there is no strength improvement (you did not get weaker), or you see no muscle growth.
If a body part is lagging behind, increase the working sets for that muscle only. Start with 2 extra working sets for 4 weeks and see if you notice a strength gain.

If you find that a body part is lagging, do that muscle first in the session. For example, if your shoulders lag, on the shoulder-dominant push day do your shoulder volume first and finish with chest. This works for any lagging muscle group.

guide.heading: Warm-up sets
body: Do 3 warm-up sets: one with the bar, one with 50%, and the last with 75% of the weight you plan on hitting on your first working set.

guide.heading: Rest between sets
body: Research suggests you may only need 1-2 minutes of rest between sets to maximize muscle growth, but the best rest depends on the exercise.
Heavy compound exercises (squats, deadlifts, presses, lunges): rest 3-5 minutes.
Lighter compound exercises (lat pulldowns, rows, leg presses, dumbbell presses): rest 2-3 minutes.
Isolation exercises (curls, lateral raises, pushdowns, leg curls, leg extensions, calf raises): rest 1-2 minutes, once the muscle feels recovered and you are no longer out of breath.
Your rest time depends on how you feel after a set and when you feel ready, so try different rest breaks and track your results to see what works for you.

guide.heading: Swapping exercises
body: You can change exercises for ones you like more, but I generally do not recommend swapping an exercise you are progressing on (no rep or strength increase means it is time to look at it). Make sure the new exercise targets the same muscles and checks the boxes in the exercise selection criteria.

Once you have found your go-to exercises, I do not recommend changing them often: it impedes progressive overload and makes progress tracking harder. If training gets boring you can absolutely swap, but only when you have to.
For 100% bodybuilding, do the Smith machine variation of all barbell movements. For rows, a chest-supported horizontal row is better than the Smith variation.

guide.heading: Training techniques used
body: RP = Rest-pause: after you reach technical failure, wait 10-15 seconds and squeeze out some more reps.
P = Long-length partials: partial reps with the target muscle at its lengthened position, at the end of a movement such as the bottom of a curl, the top of a pulldown or the bottom of a bench press.
S = Intra-set stretch: after you finish your set, stretch that muscle for 35 seconds.
Superset: do the two exercises back to back, then rest.

guide.heading: Terms
body: RIR = reps in reserve. If a set says 3 RIR, pick a weight and stop at a rep where you feel you could still push out 3 more reps.
%1RM = percentage of your one-rep max. For 80%, take 80% of your one-rep max and use that weight.
